questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis describes
questions.learningObjective: state what a formal analysis establishes from the object alone
questions.stem: A formal analysis of a painting lists its dominant colours, the direction and weight of the outlines, the placement of the main figure and the repeated shapes in the drapery. What has it established?

options.text: What is present and how the parts are arranged, established from the object alone and independent of who made it
What the painting means, since the arrangement of colour and outline carries a statement about the subject
options.misconception: conflates description with interpretation, treating arrangement as a statement

options.text: Who made it and when, since the style of the outline is the strongest evidence of a particular hand
options.misconception: assumes a formal description settles authorship, which needs comparison

options.text: How the work was made, since the visible weave of the drapery records the sequence of the workshop's technique
options.misconception: reads visible texture as a record of process rather than of surface

questions.explanation: A formal analysis is confined to what the eye can check on the object in front of it, and that confinement is its strength. Line, shape, colour, tone, texture and space can be described, and so can the ways those things are organised: where the weight falls, what repeats, where the eye is led and what interrupts it. All of that is available without knowing the name of the maker, the patron or the subject, which is why it is the first move in any examination and the last resort when documents are lost. Its limit is the mirror of its virtue. Description is not interpretation: nothing in a list of colours says what the picture is for, and the same arrangement can be produced by a workshop, an imitator or a restorer. Style is visible but not diagnostic on its own, and texture records a surface rather than a sequence of working.
questions.hint: Ask what an examiner could write down with the object in front of them and no other information.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: state why description alone cannot establish authorship
questions.stem: Two paintings of a saint have been described formally in almost identical terms: the same silhouette, the same heavy drapery folds, the same dark ground. Why does that description not settle who painted either?

options.text: Because formal features are shared and imitable, so a description of arrangement fits many hands and needs comparison
Because a formal description is only ever a summary, and a summary is too coarse to be evidence of anything
options.misconception: dismisses description as too coarse, rather than insufficient on its own

options.text: Because the two paintings are on panels of different sizes, and size prevents any comparison of their handling
options.misconception: supposes a difference of support blocks comparison of style

options.text: Because the saint is the same in both, so a description of a shared subject cannot describe the hand
options.misconception: makes the subject rather than the shared style the obstacle to comparison

questions.explanation: The features a formal description records are not private to one person. A silhouette, a fold of drapery and a dark ground belong to a vocabulary that is learned, shared and deliberately imitated, and the conventions of a workshop or a region can hold them steady across generations. So a formal description identifies a way of working rather than an individual, and it becomes evidence of authorship only when it is compared with a body of securely attributed work, where the features that recur in one hand and not in another can be found. A shared subject is not the obstacle, since two painters can treat one subject in markedly different ways, and the size of a support is irrelevant to a comparison of handling. Nor is description worthless; it is one term in an argument rather than the whole of it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the features a description records can be learned and repeated by another hand.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an iconographic reading identifies
questions.learningObjective: state that iconography identifies a subject through conventional attributes
questions.stem: A painted figure is shown holding a large key, wearing a book at the belt, and standing beside a pair of wings. What is an iconographic reading doing with those three things?

options.text: Identifying the subject by matching the attributes to a shared convention, since key and wings are known signs
Dating the painting, since particular objects came into common use only after a certain point in the century
options.misconception: treats a conventional attribute as a chronological marker

options.text: Naming the sitter, since a key and a book show the person depicted held a position of trust
options.misconception: reads a conventional sign as a possession identifying a real sitter

options.text: Setting the price, since the quality of the key and the book indicates the workshop that supplied the panel
options.misconception: supplies a valuation from the objects painted in the picture

questions.explanation: Iconography is a system of signs with rules, and the rules are learned rather than discovered. A key and a pair of wings are conventional attributes: they carry a subject's identity in the way a code carries a word, and the code has a history, a geography and a set of local variants. A reading that matches the attributes to the code can therefore identify a figure with real confidence, and where two candidates fit, a third attribute is usually what settles it. What the code does not carry is the individual. A saint is painted with a key because that is the key in the code, not because he was holding one, and wings are a sign rather than a report of an incident. Dates and values come from elsewhere: from documents, materials and comparison with securely dated work.
questions.hint: Ask whether the key belongs to the person in the picture or to the code the picture follows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Attributes used to settle a subject
questions.learningObjective: apply an iconographic code to choose between two candidate subjects
questions.stem: A figure in a panel is described as carrying a sword, a wheel broken at one side, and a book, and as wearing a crown. A second candidate subject also carries a book. Which attribute settles the reading?

options.text: The broken wheel, since it is a sign attached to the first subject alone, while book and crown are shared
The book, since a book is a sign of learning and the second subject is the one painted with books
options.misconception: leans on an attribute the description gives to both candidates

options.text: The sword, since a sword shows a figure who died violently and so narrows the subject to a martyr
options.misconception: infers a manner of death from an attribute, which is not how the code works

options.text: The crown, since a crown marks a royal subject and so rules out both of the saintly candidates
options.misconception: supplies a ruling attribute where the description gives the crown to both

questions.explanation: The logic of the code is a logic of distinctiveness. Some signs are general: a book marks learning, devotion or authority, and a crown marks rank, and both of those are attached to far more subjects than the two in question, so neither can discriminate between them. Others are specific. A wheel, and above all a wheel broken by the instrument of the martyrdom, is a sign attached to one subject in the tradition and to no other, and a sword belongs to a family of military and judicial figures. When a reading chooses between two candidates, the attribute that belongs to exactly one of them carries the identification, and the general attributes enrich the description afterwards rather than making the choice. A code is not a syllogism about causation, and no sign records how a figure died except where the tradition made that its content.
questions.hint: Ask which of the attributes belongs to one subject alone and which are shared across many.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a contextual reading brings
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence a contextual reading adds to description
questions.stem: A contextual reading brings in the patron, the occasion, the intended place, the audience and the date. What kind of evidence is that, compared with a formal analysis?

options.text: External and documentary, since it comes from records and from the setting rather than from the visible object
Internal and visual, since the patron and the occasion are recorded in the arrangement of the figures
options.misconception: treats contextual facts as legible in the arrangement rather than in records

options.text: Comparative only, since context is established by setting the work beside others of the same period
options.misconception: reduces context to stylistic comparison and excludes documents

options.text: Testimonial, since the meaning of a work is settled by what the first viewers said it was for
options.misconception: takes contemporary testimony as decisive when the first viewers often guessed

questions.explanation: Context is everything the object itself does not say. A formal analysis reads the surface; a contextual reading goes outside the object to the records around it and to the place it stood in, since a panel made for the altar end of a chapel and one made for a private room are not the same object with two addresses. The evidence is documentary, and it has the usual documentary weaknesses: inventories describe what was valued, accounts describe what was owed, and a commission letter describes what a patron wanted rather than what a painter delivered. That is a strength as much as a problem, because a conflict between two records is itself information. Style comparison belongs alongside context rather than in place of it, and the first viewers of a work are frequently the people who knew least about what it meant.
questions.hint: Ask where the patron and the intended place come from, and whether any of it is written on the object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission record as evidence
questions.learningObjective: read a payment record for what it does and does not prove
questions.stem: A surviving record names a painter, a subject, a sum of money and a date, and states that an altarpiece was to be delivered to a named chapel. What does it prove?

options.text: That an agreement existed on those terms, while the panel's present condition, its assistants and its later history stay open
That the panel now in the chapel was made under the agreement, since a chapel receives one altarpiece
options.misconception: assumes identity between a commissioned work and a surviving one

options.text: That the painter executed the whole work alone, since no assistants are named in the record
options.misconception: reads silence about assistants as proof that there were none

options.text: That the subject was painted exactly as described, since a written specification fixes the finished image
options.misconception: treats a commission line as a description of the delivered image

questions.explanation: The value of a commission record is that it evidences an agreement, and its limit is that an agreement is not the object. It fixes parties, terms, subject and date, and that is a great deal: it anchors the work in a transaction with a named price, which is one of the few firm facts available about the status of art. It does not follow that the surviving panel is the one the agreement produced, because an altarpiece can be replaced, and it certainly does not follow that one person made it, since a payment names the contractor and the shop that did the work is part of the bargain. Nor is a subject a design. A patron who wrote down what he wanted has recorded a wish, and a painter will have written it into the panel in his own way, which is usually the more interesting evidence of the two.
questions.hint: Ask whether an agreement and the object that resulted from it are the same kind of thing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in a biographical reading
questions.learningObjective: state why a biographical reading of a work is a reduction
questions.stem: An exhibition text says the painter's grief at a death in his family explains the melancholy of the figures in a portrait. What is the problem with that reading?

options.text: It uses the life to stand in for the work, and the life itself is often known only from records written for other purposes
It is too long, since an exhibition text has a few words and cannot hold an account of a painter's circumstances
options.misconception: treats the objection as one of length rather than of inference

options.text: It is too short, since a portrait cannot carry an argument that depends on a documented death outside it
options.misconception: treats the objection as one of compression rather than of inference

options.text: It is unfalsifiable, since no later evidence could show that the painter was in fact content at the time
options.misconception: claims the claim is unfalsifiable, when it is testable and usually untested

questions.explanation: A biographical reading is a reduction, because it substitutes a known cause for a visible effect and treats the effect as the symptom of the cause. A melancholy figure in a portrait is a formal and iconographic fact, and the painter's grief is a hypothesis about where it came from; the two can coincide without one explaining the other, and the same painter produced joyful, furious and neutral figures in the same decade, which is the observation that ought to embarrass a purely biographical account. There is a second problem inside the sentence: the life is not well known. A death is documented, a marriage is documented, and what either was felt is inferred from the record's tone, so the explanation rests on one inference built on another. It is not untestable, and it is not unprovable in principle, but it is a claim that needs a control group and seldom gets one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same painter behaved the same way in works made before the event, and where the grief is documented.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The assumption inside a psychological reading
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption a psychological reading requires
questions.stem: A critic writes that the repeated knotting of the hands in a group of portraits shows the sitters' anxiety. What must that reading assume before it can start?

options.text: That the hands were chosen and handled by the person whose state is being read, rather than by a formula shared across the workshop
That the portraits were painted from life in one sitting, since a drawn arrangement would not record a state of mind
options.misconception: assumes a single sitting as a precondition, when the assumption concerns the hands

options.text: That the sitters understood how their hands would be read, since anxiety read on the hands is a code they were following
options.misconception: supplies conscious convention where the reading assumes involuntary expression

options.text: That no later hand has retouched the portraits, since a repainted hand would show a modern state of mind
options.misconception: makes a restorer's condition a limit on what the critic may infer

questions.explanation: Every psychological reading of a work rests on a claim about who produced the evidence. Here it is that the knotting of the hands is a personal choice and an involuntary disclosure. That claim has to be earned, and in most cases it cannot be. Knitted hands are a formula: they appear in commissions, in workshop practice, in copies after older models and in portraits by artists with no interest in the psychology of their sitters, and a formula repeats because it is useful and legible rather than because it reveals. The moment a student is told that an unnamed assistant painted the faces while a master set the type, the inference has no seat. A second and quieter assumption is that the maker meant the hands to be read this way, which is an argument about intention that the critic is usually making on the maker's behalf. What survives is not the psychology but a better question about the convention.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the hands, and whether that choice is personal or part of a repeated way of painting.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An ideological reading stated as a claim
questions.learningObjective: state what an ideological reading asserts about power
questions.stem: A reading argues that a group of portraits showing the sitters as landowners, with their mills and their new houses, was commissioned by a class whose authority depended on being seen as bringing prosperity. What is the claim?

options.text: That the imagery is part of making and legitimising power, so the question is what the display asserted and for whom
That the portraits are propaganda in the modern sense, made deliberately to deceive a population they did not consult
options.misconception: borrows a term for modern state propaganda and applies it to a private commission

options.text: That the sitters were personally corrupt, since showing mills and houses is only done by those who profited unfairly
options.misconception: turns a claim about representation into a claim about the moral character of the sitters

options.text: That the works were unpopular, since an image made to legitimate its subjects cannot also be admired by the people who saw it
options.misconception: claims the audience rejected the image, which is not what legitimacy implies

questions.explanation: An ideological reading asks what a work does in relation to power, and the question it asks is not about the intentions of the painter but about the claim the image makes and the audience it addresses. Here the claim is specific: prosperity made visible and attached to a person, so that the ownership of mills and the rebuilding of houses reads as a contribution rather than as extraction. That is a claim about representation, and it can be examined in the objects themselves, in the hands the sitters hold, in what is present in the room and what is left out of it, and in where the pictures were hung. Calling it propaganda imports a modern apparatus of state persuasion and a modern assumption of a deceived public. And the reading is not a verdict on the sitters: a commission can make a genuine claim, be a fair account of improvement, and still serve an interest, and separating those three things is the work of a good ideological reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the image asserts about who is responsible for the prosperity, and for whose benefit that is said.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reception history as a change of meaning
questions.learningObjective: state how later history alters the reading of a work
questions.stem: A work is rediscovered in a damaged state, cut into two, rejoined, and displayed for a century in a setting that does not resemble the one it was made for. What does reception history track?

options.text: Everything that has happened to the work since it was made, and therefore how its condition and its framing have changed what it can be seen to be
Only the opinions of critics, since a work's meaning is the sum of what has been written about it over the years
options.misconception: reduces reception to commentary and ignores condition, display and ownership

options.text: Nothing, since the work's meaning was fixed when it was made and later history cannot alter it
options.misconception: claims a fixed meaning, which is what reception history exists to test

options.text: The artist's reputation, since reception history is the record of how a reputation rises and falls with each rediscovery
options.misconception: confuses the history of a work with the history of a reputation

questions.explanation: Reception history is the history of the object as an object, and it includes everything that is not the act of making. Here that is a lot: a work cut in two is a work with a seam through the middle of a figure, and the seam is now part of what anyone sees. A century in the wrong setting is a second change, because a work is partly specified by what it is next to, by the light it was made to receive and the scale it was made to be seen at, and a rehang undoes all of it. So the meaning available to a viewer today is the meaning of the object as it now stands, not the meaning of the object as first made, and the two must be distinguished before either is described. The reputation of the artist is a different history, and so is a file of critical opinion; both matter, but neither is the record of what has actually happened to this panel.
questions.hint: Ask what has physically and physically-situated happened to the object since it was finished.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reception after a relocation
questions.learningObjective: analyse how relocation and a catalogue entry reassign a work's meaning
questions.stem: A carved figure is taken from a public building in 1907 and set in a private house, where it is lit from below and seen from a single point. A catalogue entry of 1912 calls it a portrait of a named individual. What has changed?

options.text: The setting changed what the figure could be seen to be, and the catalogue supplied an identification that has to be tested rather than assumed
The figure has become a copy, since a work moved out of its original building is by definition a later replacement
options.misconception: infers copy status from a change of location

options.text: Nothing that can be assessed, since a carved figure is a fixed object and setting cannot alter its meaning
options.misconception: claims setting has no effect on how an object is read

options.text: The identification is settled, since a catalogue entry made near the time of the removal is better evidence than any later account
options.misconception: accepts a single early catalogue as conclusive

questions.explanation: Two things happened here and they are different in kind. The physical re-siting is a change in the conditions of viewing: a figure carved for a public building was composed for a particular distance, direction and scale, and lighting it from below at a single point produces a reading that the original placement would not have supported. That is a change in the object as experienced, and it is permanent. The catalogue entry is a change in the claim, not in the object: a 1912 writer had reasons to identify a figure as a named person, including the wish to make a private object legible, and an entry of that date is close to the event without being independent of it. Both belong in a reception history, and the difference between them is the difference between evidence of what an object now does and evidence of what it is.
questions.hint: Ask which change happened to the object and which happened only to the account of it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an attribution rests on
questions.learningObjective: state the independent kinds of evidence behind an attribution
questions.stem: A painting bears a signature, appears in an inventory of 1740, and matches the handling of a group of securely attributed works. On what does the attribution rest?

options.text: On three independent kinds of evidence, and its strength is their agreement rather than any one of them alone
On the signature, since a painter's own hand in the corner outweighs every other kind of evidence
options.misconception: makes a signature the decisive evidence, though it is the easiest to add

options.text: On the inventory, since a document of a stated date cannot be mistaken in the way a style can
options.misconception: treats a document as incapable of error, ignoring copies and later insertions

options.text: On the style alone, since a painter's manner is the only evidence that survives the loss of every record
options.misconception: credits style as sufficient on its own, though it is imitable

questions.explanation: An attribution is an argument from several kinds of evidence, and the reason scholars distrust any one of them is that each has a characteristic failure. A signature can be added by a later owner, a dealer, a restorer or a forger, and it sometimes records a sitter or a commissioner rather than a painter. A provenance document can describe a different work, can be a later copy of an earlier record, or can be genuine and still refer to a lost version of the panel. Style comparison is the strongest kind when the corpus is large and the hand is distinctive, and the weakest when a manner is shared or imitated. What raises a claim from guesswork to working attribution is convergence: independent lines pointing the same way, each checked against its own failure mode. Agreement is the point, and a case resting on one kind of evidence is resting on its weakest leg.
questions.hint: Ask how each kind of evidence can go wrong, and why that makes agreement between them decisive.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why one document is not enough
questions.learningObjective: explain why a single line of documentary evidence cannot carry an attribution
questions.stem: An attribution rests on a single inventory line of 1740 that names a painter and a subject, with nothing else supporting it. What is the state of the claim?

options.text: A dated documentary anchor that needs corroboration, since the entry may describe a copy, another work or a later insertion
A settled attribution, since a dated record naming a painter is stronger than any stylistic comparison
options.misconception: treats one document as conclusive and comparison as unnecessary

options.text: A settled date with an open maker, since the record fixes when the work existed but not who was responsible for it
options.misconception: supposes a document can separate the two questions when the line names both

options.text: No claim at all, since an inventory records what a collector thought valuable rather than what was true
options.misconception: dismisses a dated record as worthless because collectors are imperfect

questions.explanation: A single line is a starting point, and its date is what makes it valuable: it establishes that a work answering to this description existed in 1740, which is a real constraint on any later dating. Three things then have to be checked before the name can be carried over. The entry may describe a copy rather than the panel, and a collector's inventory is a description of an object, not a photograph of it. It may describe an object that has since been lost, while the panel in hand is a version of it. And the physical document may be a later transcript or insertion, so the handwriting and the paper want looking at. None of this makes the line worthless; it makes the line one term. A dated record plus a technical result plus a comparison with a coherent body of attributed work is a different kind of statement, and it is the combination that a catalogue is entitled to assert.
questions.hint: Ask what an inventory actually describes, and what would have to be true for the panel in hand to be that object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What can revise an attribution
questions.learningObjective: identify the evidence that moves an attribution to a different hand
questions.stem: An attribution is revised when new evidence appears. Which of these is capable of doing that?

options.text: A document naming the work, or a technical result inconsistent with the attributed hand, since each adds an independent kind of evidence
A new opinion from a scholar, since an attribution is a judgement and a better reader may simply judge differently
options.misconception: treats a change of opinion as new evidence

options.text: A more attractive attribution, since the value of a work depends on whose name it carries and a revision raises it
options.misconception: makes the value of a name the reason for revising an attribution

options.text: A cleaner picture, since a work that has been restored and cleaned can finally be seen to belong to the master
options.misconception: assumes cleaning restores a lost authorship rather than a lost surface

questions.explanation: A revision has to be caused by evidence, and the evidence has to be of a kind the original claim did not have. A document that names the work, a panel that turns out to be a copy, an underdrawing whose hand differs from the paint above it, a pigment that could not exist when the work is said to have been made, a tree-ring date later than the attributed career: each of these adds a line that the earlier attribution either ignored or did not have. A fresh opinion is a different matter. Opinions change as the corpus grows, and that is normal and healthy, but it is a shift in the balance of an argument rather than new material in it, and a case that is reversed on taste alone has not been shown to have been wrong. A cleaning can clarify a work enormously, and what it clarifies is the surface, not the maker.
questions.hint: Ask whether the new information is a fact about the object or a fresh verdict about it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two independent lines revising a hand
questions.learningObjective: analyse a revision driven by technical and documentary evidence together
questions.stem: A painting long given to a master is shown on X-radiography to contain a second, differently composed figure beneath the paint, and a record is then found describing a copy of that composition made for a patron abroad. What does the combination do?

options.text: It moves the work towards the workshop or a copy, because an earlier composition and an external copy both point away from the attributed hand
It proves the painting is a forgery, since a changed composition and a copy of it are both signs of deliberate deceit
options.misconception: jumps to forgery, where changing a composition is ordinary practice

options.text: It dates the work precisely, since the second figure fixes the moment the master abandoned his first arrangement
options.misconception: reads an abandoned composition as a precise date for the work

options.text: It leaves the attribution untouched, since a changed composition is normal in a panel and a copy abroad proves nothing about the original
options.misconception: ignores two independent lines that both point the same way

questions.explanation: What makes this a strong revision is that the two lines are independent of each other and point the same way. A composition under the paint says the panel was reused, which is common: an artist or workshop begins with a design and abandons it, and a second composition on the same panel is a fact about working practice rather than about deceit. A record of a copy of that composition made for a patron abroad says the design was circulated, which is what happens to a successful arrangement. Together they make a coherent account in which the surviving panel is a version rather than the original of a design the attributed master did not execute, and each line corroborates the other. Neither line alone would move the attribution as far, and neither is a proof of forgery: forgery requires an intention to deceive, and no one has established that here.
questions.hint: Ask what each line of evidence can be explained by, and whether the two explanations are the same one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What connoisseurship vocabulary grades
questions.learningObjective: state what the terms of attribution are doing in a catalogue
questions.stem: Catalogue entries distinguish between autograph, workshop, circle of, follower of, after, copy and pastiche. What is that vocabulary doing?

options.text: Grading the relationship claimed between a work and a named person, so that each term is a different assertion with a different burden of proof
Ranking the works by merit, so that an autograph is better than a copy in the way one object is better than another
options.misconception: reads the terms as a quality ranking rather than a claim about authorship

options.text: Recording the degree of damage, so that a workshop is used for a work that has lost its original surface
options.misconception: confuses the terms with condition categories

options.text: Keeping the older attributions for reference, so that a superseded name is printed alongside the current one
options.misconception: treats the vocabulary as a record of superseded attributions

questions.explanation: Every term in that list is a sentence about a relationship, and the sentences differ enormously in what they assert. Autograph claims the hand of the named person, which needs the strongest evidence. Workshop claims that the person was responsible while assistants executed much of the work, which is a normal condition of a large commission rather than a demotion. Circle of and follower of claim proximity, in time, place or milieu, without claiming the hand at all. After claims derivation from a known work, so it can be centuries later and the prototype has to be identified. Copy and pastiche name behaviours rather than hands. The purpose of the vocabulary is precision about what is being claimed, so that two readers can disagree about a specific term instead of arguing past each other about the work in general.
questions.hint: Ask what statement each term makes about the hand, and how far each reaches.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The gap between circle of and after
questions.learningObjective: distinguish proximity of milieu from derivation from a known work
questions.stem: A work is catalogued as circle of a named painter, and another as after that painter. What separates the two descriptions?

options.text: The first claims closeness in time and milieu without claiming the hand, while the second claims derivation from an identified work
The first is used for paintings and the second for sculpture, so the distinction is one of medium rather than of claim
options.misconception: supplies a media rule the vocabulary does not have

options.text: The first is an older label and the second a newer one, so the change marks a trend in cataloguing practice
options.misconception: reads a change in usage as the difference in the terms

options.text: The first is a courtesy title and the second a finding, so only the second is a considered opinion about authorship
options.misconception: dismisses the first as empty flattery when it is a measured claim

questions.explanation: The two terms sit at different distances from the person named. Circle of is a claim about milieu: the work was made by somebody who belonged to the same world as the painter, trained in the same place, at the same moment, and the evidence is comparative, showing that the work shares features with securely attributed pieces without sharing the personal habits of the hand. After is a claim about derivation: there is a prototype, a known composition, and the catalogued work follows it, which means the two may be separated by a generation or by a century. That is why an after needs its prototype named, since without one the term is empty, and why a circle of is a positive description of context rather than a softener for indecision. Neither term ranks the work, and both can be revised as the corpus grows.
questions.hint: Ask whether each term needs a known prototype, and what kind of closeness each is claiming.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a condition report records
questions.learningObjective: interpret a condition report as a dated baseline
questions.stem: A report records a four centimetre tear at the lower edge with associated losses, two areas of lifting paint, an old repair visible in raking light, and a discoloured rectangle where a frame rebate once sat. What does the report establish?

options.text: A dated, itemised state of the object, including damage, earlier intervention and evidence of how it was once framed
The value of the panel, since the extent of the losses and the quality of the colour set what an object is worth
options.misconception: reads a condition record as a valuation

options.text: That the panel was made for a church, since the rebate shows it was fitted into a fixed architectural setting
options.misconception: reads a rebate as proof of a particular kind of original site

options.text: That the old repair was badly done, since a repair that remains visible after this long has failed in its purpose
options.misconception: equates visibility with failure, when visible repair is the point

questions.explanation: A condition report is a baseline, and its whole value lies in being dated and itemised. Each entry is a fact about the object at a known moment: how much is torn and where, where the paint has lifted, what has already been done to it by an earlier restorer, and what the surface still records of its past. The discoloured rectangle is the sort of entry that is easy to skip and hard to replace: it says the panel once had a rebate of a particular size, which is physical evidence of its earlier housing and a starting point for any argument about where it stood. A report is not a valuation, and a frame rebate by itself does not decide between a church and a private room. And a repair that is still visible in raking light has done its job exactly as intended, since the aim of a repair is to be findable by a conservator and invisible to everyone else.
questions.hint: Ask what each line of the report is evidence of, and what a report is a record of rather than an assessment of.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A before and after pair of reports
questions.learningObjective: interpret paired reports as a record of intervention
questions.stem: A second report made after treatment records the tear mended with a fill that remains visible in raking light, the lifting consolidated, the old earlier repair left in place and written into the new report. What does the pair of reports show?

options.text: That the treatment is documented and distinguishable, so a later conservator can see what was done and can undo it
That the object was restored beyond usefulness, since a visible fill has been added to a surface that was previously complete
options.misconception: treats a distinguishable fill as damage rather than as documented repair

options.text: That the old repair should have been removed, since leaving an earlier intervention in place compromises the new one
options.misconception: supposes earlier repairs must be removed, when the practice is to record them

options.text: That the tear was old, since a recent break would have left fresh losses along the edge of the fill
options.misconception: reads the age of a tear from the finish of a repair rather than from the earlier report

questions.explanation: Two reports, before and after, turn a treatment into a record, and that is what reversibility looks like in practice. The fill is visible in raking light, which means a conservator in fifty years can find it, identify what was used, and remove it if the materials then available are better than the ones used now. Consolidation, by contrast, is the part of the treatment that cannot be fully undone, and it is a decision made because the alternative is losing paint. The decision to leave the earlier repair in place and describe it in the new report is the same principle applied to history: a previous intervention is part of the object now, and removing it would be a further, less reversible change. What the pair cannot do is tell you when the tear happened, because the age of damage comes from the first report, not from the finish of the fill.
questions.hint: Ask what a later conservator needs to find in order to undo or repeat a treatment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a condition report does not settle
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of a condition report
questions.stem: A condition report describes every loss, stain and previous repair on a panel in precise terms. What can it not establish?

options.text: The maker, the value, or what the panel looked like when new, since all of those need evidence of a different kind
The current state of the object, since a report written on the table cannot record what is happening inside the panel
options.misconception: dismisses the report's central function, which is to record current state

options.text: Which treatment is needed, since a report records damage without proposing any response to it
options.misconception: misses that a report is normally written to inform a treatment decision

options.text: Whether the object is worth conserving, since a poor report is a sign that the object has not been valued
options.misconception: infers an owner's valuation from the existence of a report

questions.explanation: A condition report is a technical record and it is silent on three questions that people often hope it will answer. It does not identify a maker, because that needs comparison and documents. It does not value the object, because a value is a relation between an object and a market at a moment, and a report is not a market. And it does not reconstruct an original appearance, though it can supply the evidence for a careful reconstruction: the rebate shows a former frame, a discoloured area shows where light fell, and a fill records a loss. Those reconstructions are arguments with a stated basis, which is the strongest form the claim can take. What the report does do is set the terms for every later decision, since a treatment is judged against the baseline it was written on, and a second report is only meaningful because the first one exists.
questions.hint: Ask which of these questions would be settled by looking at the panel at all.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a technical analysis consists of
questions.learningObjective: state what physical methods contribute to an examination
questions.stem: A technical examination includes imaging, elemental analysis, microscopy of paint films and the dating of timber. What does this body of methods contribute?

options.text: Facts about the materials and their sequence, which are checkable and largely independent of who made the object
A judgement about the artist's intention, since the materials used are the clearest evidence of what was planned
options.misconception: reads material facts as evidence of intention

options.text: A value, since a panel with a documented tree-ring date can be priced from the date alone
options.misconception: supplies a valuation from a material result

options.text: A single conclusive answer, since an instrument reading settles the question the object was being asked about
options.misconception: expects a single instrumental answer to an open question

questions.explanation: The contribution of physical methods is that they produce facts with a small number of ways of being wrong. Imaging shows what lies beneath a surface; elemental analysis says which materials are present and in what proportion; a cross-section shows the order in which a picture was built up; a ring measurement says when a tree stopped growing. Each of those can be repeated by somebody else on the same object, which is what gives the result its standing. What they do not do is answer the question that was asked. A pigment is not a plan, a ring date is not a maker, and an instrument reports what is there rather than what it means. Used well, the methods fix a sequence and a set of constraints, and interpretation is then done with those constraints in hand rather than in their place.
questions.hint: Ask what an instrument measures, and whether the measurement is the same thing as the question.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit of physical evidence
questions.learningObjective: state why sampling and sensitivity bound a technical result
questions.stem: An elemental reading of one small area of a panel finds no lead white, and a report concludes that lead white was not used in the painting. Why is that conclusion unsafe?

options.text: Because the instrument reads the spot it is aimed at, and a pigment absent from one point may be present everywhere else
Because lead white is the most common pigment in European painting and so its absence is a technical impossibility
options.misconception: makes a common pigment physically necessary, when it is a convention

options.text: Because the report should have used a different instrument, since elemental analysis is not the right method for a panel
options.misconception: blames the method rather than the sample size

options.text: Because a negative reading means the panel was repainted, since a second campaign always removes the earlier pigment
options.misconception: infers repainting from a negative reading at one point

questions.explanation: Physical methods are local by nature. An elemental reading is aimed at a point, a sample removes a fragment, and an image records what lies under a particular patch of paint; none of them speaks for an object as a whole. So a negative result is a statement about the sample, and a panel painting frequently contains a white in the flesh, another in a highlight and none in the sky, which is a normal outcome of mixing rather than a contradiction. This is why reports state where a sample was taken and how many, and why a claim about the whole picture requires a set of readings across it. A pigment is also not a single substance: lead white is a mixture, and a reading that reports lead but not tin may be reporting the layer beneath or the layer above. None of this makes the method useless; it makes a conclusion wider than the sample unsound.
questions.hint: Ask how large a piece of the picture the instrument actually looked at.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What infrared reflectography shows
questions.learningObjective: state what infrared reflectography reveals and why
questions.stem: Infrared reflectography is used on a panel painting and brings up a drawn figure that differs from the painted one. Why does the drawing show?

options.text: Because a carbon-based line absorbs infrared and stays dark, so a drawing under a paint that transmits the light is revealed
Because infrared is more penetrating than visible light, so it passes through the panel and photographs the drawing on the reverse
options.misconception: puts the drawing on the back of the panel, where the method does not reach

options.text: Because infrared makes old paint fluoresce, so a covered line is revealed by the glow of the layer above it
options.misconception: describes fluorescence, which is an ultraviolet technique

options.text: Because the paint above a drawing is always thinner, and thin paint lets more infrared through to the line
options.misconception: makes the effect a property of paint thickness, when it is a property of the drawing material

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a property of two materials. Carbon-based drawing lines, such as black chalk or an ink of soot, absorb the longer infrared wavelengths that the eye cannot see, so when the panel is illuminated in the infrared and imaged, the buried line stays dark while the paint over it, which transmits, is read as bright. The result is a drawing that can be seen in position and often read, and it is one of the few techniques that can recover a design from under a finished surface. What it does not do is see everything. A line drawn in a colour that reflects infrared, such as a red chalk, can be invisible to the method, and a thick or dark overlying paint can hide a line that is present. The differences the technique exposes are therefore suggestive and need comparison with documents and with other images before they carry a conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what the dark line is made of, and what infrared light does when it meets that material.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an X-radiograph shows
questions.learningObjective: state why radiography reveals dense materials and what that reveals
questions.stem: An X-radiograph of a canvas shows a grid of small metal points and a large pale mass across the lower third. What do those two features indicate?

options.text: Fixings and a dense lead-containing material, since metal and lead absorb the beam and appear pale in the image
Dirt and a tear, since damaged areas let more of the beam through and so appear pale
options.misconception: inverts the reading of density, since a loss lets more beam through

options.text: A grid of overpaint and a water stain, since both absorb the beam more than the surrounding film
options.misconception: supplies paint-related features where the points are metal fixings

options.text: The stretcher bars and the frame rebate, since both are denser than the canvas and cast the pale shapes seen
options.misconception: attributes the features to the support rather than to the paint and fixings

questions.explanation: A radiograph is a shadow picture of absorption, and that is all it is. X-rays pass through organic material readily and are stopped to a greater or lesser degree by anything with heavy atoms in it, so a metal fixing and a lead-containing white paint both absorb more of the beam than the ground behind them and read as pale shapes against a darker field. A regular grid of small points across a canvas is the standard evidence of the tacks that fixed the fabric to its strainer, often together with the seams where the widths of the canvas were joined, and those are construction facts about the object rather than features of the picture. Because the image registers density, a radiograph can also show a composition that was painted out, a heavy layer where a passage was reworked, and the lead weights of a later lining, which is why it is used as a record of the object's history as well as of its making.
questions.hint: Ask which materials absorb the beam, and what a metal fixing would look like in the image.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An underdrawing read against the paint
questions.learningObjective: analyse a described divergence between underdrawing and paint
questions.stem: Infrared reflectography of a panel shows a face drawn with the head tilted sharply to one side, and the painted head above it turns the other way, in a pose that matches a figure in another surviving work. What does that combination support?

options.text: That the drawn design was changed in the paint, and that the final pose was taken from an existing model rather than invented
That the underdrawing is by a different, more skilled hand, since a competent designer would not have drawn a head the other way
options.misconception: treats a changed design as evidence of a different, better draughtsman

options.text: That the panel is a copy, since a pose borrowed from another work can only be a copy of that work
options.misconception: leaps from borrowing a pose to copying a whole object

options.text: That the two works were painted in the same campaign, since a shared pose proves a shared commission and date
options.misconception: reads a common source as proof of a common occasion

questions.explanation: Two findings, each modest, and together they support a claim that neither would support alone. A drawing and a paint that disagree on a pose is an ordinary event: the design is set, the panel is prepared, the pose is reconsidered in the light of the figure, and the final arrangement is painted over the first. That it is the other way round in the paint shows a change of mind, and it also tells you where the change happened in the working process. A painted pose that matches a figure in another surviving work is a borrowing, which is a normal part of working from a model, a print or another painter, and it explains where the alternative pose came from. What it does not establish is that the panel is a copy, since copying a pose is not copying a work, and it does not establish a shared commission, since a shared source is a common arrangement in a workshop tradition.
questions.hint: Ask what a painter normally does when a design is reconsidered, and what borrowing a pose implies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A radiograph read for an earlier composition
questions.learningObjective: interpret radiography as a record of revision
questions.stem: A radiograph of a large canvas shows a tall shape occupying the left third, where the visible painting has open sky, and a grid of tacks along three edges with a fourth edge bare. What has happened?

options.text: The canvas was first used for a taller composition and was cut down, with the bare edge marking where a strip was removed
The sky was painted over an earlier landscape, since a tall shape in open sky must be a tree or a building
options.misconception: assumes a subject, when the geometry of the edges is the stronger evidence

options.text: The tacks show the canvas was relined, since a new set of fixings means a new support behind the old one
options.misconception: reads a missing row of fixings as evidence of relining

options.text: The work is unfinished, since a radiograph with an unpainted area shows the painter stopped before finishing the left side
options.misconception: reads a pale radiograph area as missing paint in the visible painting

questions.explanation: The radiograph is describing the history of the object, and the three findings describe it together. A tall dense mass under what is now open sky is the ghost of a composition that was painted and then painted out, and the paint above it that covers it is the evidence of the change. The tack pattern is the stronger clue: fixings along three edges and none along the fourth mean the canvas was not made for this stretcher as it now stands, and the untacked edge is where the material stops. That is a cut, and a cut on three sides of a rectangular canvas reduces it to a smaller shape, which accounts for the truncated composition above. The sky is a present fact and not a loss, so the painting is finished, and a set of fixings records how the object was made fast rather than what was done to it later.
questions.hint: Ask what an edge with no fixings along it means, and what would have happened to a composition that crossed it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pigment analysis as a dating constraint
questions.learningObjective: state how an identified pigment constrains a date
questions.stem: A painting is claimed to be fifteenth century, and analysis finds a pigment that was not manufactured until the nineteenth. What does the finding do?

options.text: It rules out the claim, since the material was not available to be used, and it dates the layer that contains it
It confirms the claim, since a rare pigment shows that the painter had access to valuable materials
options.misconception: reads the presence of a pigment as supporting a date

options.text: It dates the whole panel, since all the layers must have been applied at the same time
options.misconception: extends a layer's date to the whole object without evidence

options.text: It identifies the painter, since a specific pigment points to a particular workshop that used it consistently
options.misconception: supplies an attribution from a single material reading

questions.explanation: Manufacture is a hard constraint. If a colour in a layer could not be made until a particular decade, then that layer was applied after that decade, and any date proposed for it before that point is wrong. This is one of the few kinds of evidence in art history that can exclude rather than merely suggest, and it is why the appearance of a synthetic colour in a painting is treated as a serious event. The discipline required is about the layer. A panel can be painted, cleaned, relined and repainted over centuries, and analysis samples a campaign rather than an object, so the finding dates the layer that carries the pigment and leaves the rest of the object open. It is also a finding about material, not about a person: a pigment can travel, be copied, and be applied by anyone with access to it, so the reading constrains a date and says nothing by itself about a maker.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pigment could have been bought in the century claimed, and which layer was sampled.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Canvas weave as evidence of origin
questions.learningObjective: state what a weave analysis can and cannot establish
questions.stem: The threads of a canvas are counted and the weave structure and thread density are compared with surviving textiles and with recorded supplies. What can that establish?

options.text: That the fabric came from a particular source or region, and that a canvas is not later than the latest of the recorded supplies
That the canvas is the original support of the painting, since a replacement would not match a period weave
options.misconception: concludes originality from a weave match, ignoring that the fabric can be old stock

options.text: The painter's nationality, since a canvas of a given weave identifies the country the artist worked in
options.misconception: moves from material origin to the nationality of the maker

options.text: Nothing at all, since a weave is a property of a material and carries no information about where or when it was made
options.misconception: dismisses material evidence as carrying no information

questions.explanation: Textiles are made to order by regions and periods, so a canvas has a measurable signature: a thread count, a weave structure, a twist direction, sometimes a width, and a dye. Put those against a body of surviving cloth and against records of what was being sold where, and the fabric becomes evidence of supply rather than of authorship, which is what it can honestly support. It also carries a terminus: if the recorded supplies of a particular canvas in a particular town begin in one decade, a panel on that canvas cannot predate it, since the cloth came from the supply. What it cannot do is prove the support is original, because old stock was reused and because a later restorer may have chosen the period weave deliberately. Nor does a region of manufacture say anything about the nationality of the person who painted on it.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a textile traceable, and what the trace identifies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tree-ring report read for a date
questions.learningObjective: interpret a dendrochronology report for what it dates
questions.stem: A report gives the width of each ring in a panel, matches the sequence against a regional chronology, and states that the outermost preserved ring falls in the 1740s with several rings missing at the edge. What has been dated?

options.text: The tree, and with it the earliest possible felling, since the panel cannot be painted before the wood stopped growing
The painting, since the panel was prepared in the same year the tree was felled
options.misconception: confuses the felling of the tree with the making of the object

options.text: The restoration, since a later repair would have used timber of a different ring pattern
options.misconception: reads a ring match as dating a repair rather than the panel

options.text: The artist, since a dated panel narrows the possible makers to those working in that decade
options.misconception: turns a date into an attribution without any comparison of work

questions.explanation: The method works because trees in a region record the same sequence of good and bad years, so a measured sequence of ring widths can be matched against a compiled chronology, and the match places the rings in specific years. Where several rings are missing at the edge, the panel was cut from the trunk some distance inside the bark, so the report gives a limit and not a single year: the tree stood for at least as long as the missing rings, which is why a careful report says the felling cannot be earlier than a stated year. That is the terminus post quem, and it is a lower bound on the object, not a date for it. A panel can wait a decade or two for a painter, so the report bounds the making from below and says nothing about who made it, and a modern repair with different timber would not match the panel's chronology at all.
questions.hint: Ask when the tree stopped growing, and how long after that a painter could wait.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a terminus post quem does
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of the constraint a ring date places on a date
questions.stem: A panel's felling is dated to no earlier than 1748, and a painting on it is proposed for 1700. What does the measurement do to the proposal?

options.text: It excludes the proposal, because the wood the picture is on did not exist when the picture is said to have been made
It confirms the proposal's era, since a date near 1748 is close enough to 1700 to be consistent
options.misconception: treats a bound as a confirmation of any date within a century

options.text: It shows that the panel is a replacement, since an original support must always be contemporary with the paint
options.misconception: assumes support and paint must share a date rather than following one another

options.text: It fixes the painting at 1748, since a panel cannot be painted before it is felled and is painted as soon as it is
options.misconception: converts a lower bound into an exact date

questions.explanation: A terminus post quem fixes the direction of the constraint, and the direction is the whole point of the term. The wood has to be felled before it can be prepared and painted on, so the felling date rules out everything earlier and leaves everything later open. A proposal of 1700 is on the wrong side of that bound, and a felling of 1748 therefore excludes it whatever else is argued. Three errors sit either side of this one. Treating a bound as a date assumes a painter works the moment the tree comes down, when stock timber waits in a yard for years and the panel is then seasoned, prepared and painted. Assuming the panel must be contemporary with the paint repeats the same error from the other direction. And a measurement is not a condemnation of the object: it is a constraint to be reconciled, whether by redating the picture, by finding an earlier campaign on the panel, or by explaining the wood.
questions.hint: Ask in which direction the wood's date constrains the paint, and whether the two must be simultaneous.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ring date that conflicts with a paint date
questions.learningObjective: interpret a mismatch between the wood and the paint
questions.stem: A panel's outermost ring is dated to 1480, the painting is proposed for 1520, and a second board in the same frame is dated to 1520. What does the record show?

options.text: A bound the 1520 painting already satisfies, so the wood is not the constraint and the question moves to the paint
A contradiction, since a panel dated 1480 is too old for a 1520 painting and the catalogue must be corrected
options.misconception: treats a board older than a painting as a contradiction

options.text: That the painting is later than the panel, since two boards from the same tree must be cut at the same time
options.misconception: assumes boards cut from one tree must be cut together

options.text: That the dating method is unreliable, since two ring sequences in one region can be matched to the same years
options.misconception: denies the basis of the method, which is that one region shares one sequence

questions.explanation: The two results have to be read against the direction of the constraint. A ring dated to 1480 gives a lower bound: the panel cannot be painted before the wood is felled, and a painting proposed for 1520 sits comfortably after that, so the wood has excluded nothing. The second board, dated to 1520, tells you where that board's outer ring fell in the same regional sequence, and boards cut from one trunk are routinely used years apart. What the pair establishes is a consistency check that has passed, and a check passing is a real result because it removes a hypothesis. The paint date now has to be argued on its own evidence, and the ring dates are no longer the interesting part of the file. Note the direction of each error: a panel older than its painting is normal, because timber waits in a yard, and it is the panel younger than the painting that cannot be explained.
questions.hint: Ask in which direction the wood's date constrains the paint, and whether an older panel is a problem.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A panel made from older boards
questions.learningObjective: explain how reused timber produces a date mismatch
questions.stem: A small panel is described as made of two boards whose rings run in different directions, one of them knotty, and whose ring dates are eighty years earlier than the painting on them. What does that explain?

options.text: That the painter used boards already to hand, so the wood predates the picture and reuse explains the mismatch
That the panel is a modern pastiche, since nobody would have reused wood in the fifteenth century
options.misconception: supplies an implausible reason for reuse, which was routine practice

options.text: That the paint is a later addition over an abandoned panel, since a younger paint needs a younger campaign
options.misconception: infers a later campaign from the wood, when the wood may simply be old

options.text: That the panel was cut from a painted piece, since boards of mixed grain come from reused furniture
options.misconception: makes grain direction evidence of a painted source

questions.explanation: Old timber was valuable, and small panels were commonly made from whatever boards were in the workshop: offcuts, a shutter, a piece of furniture, a board already prepared. So a panel can be eighty years older than the picture on it, and the ring dates then record the wood rather than the making, which is why the two dates are not in conflict but simply about different things. Two features in the description point the same way. Rings running in different directions mean the boards were cut from different parts of the trunk or from different trees, which is what happens when the pieces are not from one plank. A knotty board is a defect a joiner avoids in a purpose-made panel and accepts in whatever is lying in the yard. Neither feature indicates a later campaign, and both are evidence of a shop making an object to order.
questions.hint: Ask whether old wood was cheap or valuable, and what a workshop would do with boards already in the yard.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A technical report read against a claim
questions.learningObjective: interpret a technical report as a range rather than a verdict
questions.stem: A report states that the ground is a chalk and glue gesso of the usual period type, that the paint contains lead white, that the underdrawing differs from the paint, and that a label is fixed to the frame and not to the panel. What does it settle?

options.text: That the materials and the design are consistent with a period practice, while the label is evidence about the frame alone
That the panel is a century earlier than the label, since a label on the object names the work of its own century
options.misconception: lets a label fixed to a frame date the panel behind it

options.text: That the panel is a copy, since a design that differs from the paint cannot have been the original design
options.misconception: treats a changed underdrawing as evidence of copying

options.text: Nothing, since a report on materials and a report on drawing are different kinds of evidence and cannot be combined
options.misconception: supposes evidence of different kinds cannot be weighed together

questions.explanation: Read the report as statements of different scope. The materials are consistent with a period practice, which is a useful compatibility result and a weak identification, since such recipes were followed for decades and adopted by imitators. The underdrawing differing from the paint is a fact about working method, and the commonest explanation is a design reconsidered in the light layer, not a copy. The label is the item to handle carefully: fixed to the frame rather than the panel, it is evidence about a frame, which is frequently a later addition, and a label is also a movable thing that can be transferred with a frame or written at any time after the object was made. The report settles a consistency and offers a distribution of possibilities; it does not deliver a verdict, and a verdict is not what physical examination is for.
questions.hint: Ask which object each piece of evidence is actually attached to, and what a change of design usually means.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two sides of a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: state the shape of the argument on each side of a dispute
questions.stem: A work is claimed for a named master because a document associates him with the commission, and is disputed because its handling does not match his accepted works. What kind of disagreement is this?

options.text: Between two kinds of evidence of unequal strength, where the document asserts a transaction and the handling is a comparison
Between two scholars of equal standing, since a disagreement about a work cannot rest on evidence
options.misconception: removes evidence from the question and leaves only authority

options.text: Between a date and a place, since documents fix where a work was made and style fixes when
options.misconception: assigns the two kinds of evidence to the wrong questions

options.text: Between a value and a technique, since a claim raises the price of a work and a comparison lowers it
options.misconception: confuses the scholarly dispute with a market effect

questions.explanation: Almost every disputed attribution is a disagreement between kinds of evidence and not between people. A document asserts a transaction: somebody agreed to be paid for something, and the document may name a subject, a place and a sum. A stylistic comparison asserts a relationship between a work and a body of work judged to share a hand, and its strength depends on how distinctive that hand is and how much comparison has been done. The two are not commensurable, which is why a dispute can stay open for decades, and the useful question is what each side would have to produce. A document claim is met by showing that the entry describes another object, that it was inserted later, or that it records a contract for a copy. A style claim is met by a securely attributed work that shares features the disputed work lacks, or by a technical result that cannot be reconciled with the hand.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of statement each kind of evidence makes, rather than who is making it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weighing evidence in a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: sequence the weighing of documentary and technical evidence
questions.stem: A work is claimed for a named master on documentary grounds and disputed on stylistic ones. First say what the document establishes, and then say what the objection has to be stronger than.

options.text: An agreement existed on those terms, and the objection must show the surviving panel cannot be the object that agreement produced
The work was painted by the master, and the objection must show a better candidate whose hand explains the handling
options.misconception: overreads a contract as proof of the finished object

options.text: Only that the work existed, and the objection need only state a preference for a different and better documented hand
options.misconception: reduces the document to bare existence and makes a preference sufficient

options.text: Nothing at all, since a document and a comparison cannot be weighed against each other in principle
options.misconception: declares the weighing impossible rather than describing how it is done

questions.explanation: The first half is what a document can carry: parties, terms, subject, date, price. It establishes a transaction and a work answering to it. The second half is the test a dispute has to meet. The document names an agreement, not an object, and between an agreement and a panel there are several ordinary explanations to exclude: the panel is a copy of a lost original, the agreement covered a different and larger work from which the panel is a fragment, the entry was inserted or copied later, or the same document is the source of several attributions. A stylistic objection becomes decisive when one of those is established, because then the transaction is real and the object in hand is not what it describes. That is why the strongest disputes combine a document with a material result, since the two answer different questions and a result about materials cannot be absorbed by a claim about paperwork.
questions.hint: Ask what sits between an agreement and the object that resulted from it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a forgery gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: identify the physical tells that distinguish a forgery from an original
questions.stem: A painting presented as fifteenth century is described as having a uniformly fine network of cracks, a ground of uniformly fine texture, and a surface in which the paint sits on the ground without the raised passages an old picture develops. What do these features suggest?

options.text: A surface made to look old rather than one that has become old, since cracking, texture and relief accumulate unevenly with time
A very well preserved fifteenth century panel, since uniform cracks and a fine ground are marks of careful early craftsmanship
options.misconception: reads evenness as early quality, when ageing is never even

options.text: A nineteenth century imitation of a fifteenth century ground, since fine grounds and thin paint belong to the later period
options.misconception: names a date from a style of ground rather than from an account of ageing

options.text: A damaged original that has been reduced, since the absence of raised passages shows the surface has been levelled
options.misconception: infers abrasion where the description gives a uniform surface

questions.explanation: Ageing is not uniform, and that is the observation the description turns on. A panel of wood moves with the seasons, thick paint in one area and thin in another dries at different rates, and a layer applied to a damp ground behaves differently from one applied to a dry one, so an original surface develops a variety of cracks of different widths, a texture that varies with the material used, and slight relief where the paint sits proud. A uniform fine network of cracks, an evenly fine ground and a flat surface have been produced deliberately, because a forger can make a chosen crack pattern easier than a real one. This is what a technical examination is for: to compare the physical behaviour of the object with what a genuine object of that date and type does. Uniformity is not by itself proof of deceit, since a restorer can produce it, but it is a reason to look at the materials and the provenance next.
questions.hint: Ask whether real ageing produces the same crack size and the same texture everywhere on a panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pastiche distinguished from forgery
questions.learningObjective: distinguish imitation for effect from imitation for deception
questions.stem: A nineteenth-century artist paints deliberately in the manner of a seventeenth master, signing with his own name and exhibiting the result as a study of that manner. What is the work, and how does it differ from a forgery?

options.text: A pastiche, since it imitates a manner openly and for its own effect, where a forgery aims to be taken for the earlier work
A forgery, since deliberately imitating an earlier manner is deception whatever the artist signs
options.misconception: makes imitation alone sufficient for forgery, ignoring intention and disclosure

options.text: A copy, since copying an earlier manner without a prototype behind it cannot be a work in its own right
options.misconception: denies that an independent work in an old manner can exist

options.text: A pastiche and a forgery at once, since the two terms have always meant the same thing in technical literature
options.misconception: asserts an identity between two terms that separate intention from effect

questions.explanation: The dividing line is intention, and it is a real one because it changes everything downstream. In a pastiche the imitation is the point: the artist is exercising a manner, often reaching back several centuries, and the work is offered as what it plainly is, which is why it carries its own date and its own signature and is discussed as a performance of a style. In a forgery the imitation is a means to an end, which is that somebody should believe the object is earlier and by somebody else, and everything about the object is bent to that end, from an invented provenance to an aged surface. This is why a pastiche is not merely a failed or a lazy version of the same activity: the pastiche is a positive achievement, and judging it by whether the manner was well copied misses the fact that nobody was being deceived. The category is unstable, because a pastiche made to be sold as the real thing is a forgery, and intention is the only thing that has changed.
questions.hint: Ask what the maker intends the viewer to believe, and what the viewer has been told.
