questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an unfinished surface shows
questions.learningObjective: read an unfinished work as a record of the order of working
questions.stem: A painting is described as finished in the upper half while the lower half shows the ground, a drawn grid, the first lay-in of a shadow and a knife-scratched correction to the drawing. What does the surface record?

options.text: The order of working, since a grid, a changed drawing and a first lay-in are stages that leave the sequence legible
The painter's illness, since a work left part-finished is the standard sign that a hand failed partway through
options.misconception: supplies a cause the surface does not record

options.text: A damaged work, since a prepared but unpainted area is the ordinary result of abrasion and loss of the paint layer
options.misconception: reads a deliberately unpainted area as loss

options.text: A collaborative hand, since a knife-scratched correction shows that a second person altered the drawing
options.misconception: treats a working correction as evidence of a second worker

questions.explanation: An unfinished work is unusually informative because it shows the process rather than hiding it, and the stages are legible in the order they were performed. A grid and a corrected drawing come before the paint, since a design has to exist before colour is laid over it, and the first lay-in of a shadow is the first act of painting, so the unfinished half tells you which parts of the composition the painter had reached. A knife-scratched correction is a working decision: a line that was drawn, judged wrong and cut into before the paint went on. None of this is damage, and none of it is evidence about a second person, since a worker correcting their own drawing is doing something entirely ordinary. What it does tell you is the point at which the work stopped, and that can be evidence about a commission, a date or a habit of working that a finished surface would have hidden.
questions.hint: Ask which of the features had to be made first, and whether a correction needs a second pair of hands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a technical examination
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a physical examination
questions.stem: A painting is to be examined physically before it goes on display. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Compare the results with the documents and with dated comparanda, and state the range of dates the evidence supports
Examine and photograph the surface in good light, recording the condition and what earlier work has left behind
Sample the smallest necessary fragments, choosing the points from what the images have already shown
Image the surface and what lies beneath it by reflected light, by infrared and by radiography, before anything is taken

questions.explanation: The order is set by the fact that the object is finite and every step changes it. So the first stage is non-invasive: look, in good light, and record what is there, because a condition made before any handling is the baseline against which every later step is judged, and because examination under raking light reveals surface relief, old repairs and lifting that flat light hides. Imaging comes next and is still non-invasive, and it earns its place before sampling for two reasons, since it shows where the interesting things are and it shows the order of campaigns, so a sample can be taken where it will answer a question rather than where it is convenient. Then sampling, as small and as few as the evidence allows, since a removed fragment cannot be put back. Only then comparison, because a result means nothing until it is read against documents and against securely dated work.
questions.hint: Ask which steps change the object and which do not, and what imaging tells you before a fragment is taken.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A campaign that the materials contradict
questions.learningObjective: state what a synthetic binder does to a proposed date
questions.stem: A painting catalogued as sixteenth century is found on cross-section to have its ground bound in a synthetic resin of the twentieth century. What does that establish?

options.text: That the layer as it now stands is later than the catalogue, so either the work or its surface history must be rewritten
That the original painting is also later, since a sixteenth century painter would have used a modern ground
options.misconception: carries a modern ground back through the layers beneath it

options.text: That the object is a forgery, since a synthetic binder is a material no earlier work could contain
options.misconception: turns a later campaign into an accusation of deception

options.text: Nothing, since binders migrate between layers over centuries and any ground can be found in a later film
options.misconception: supplies a migration that the analysis of a specific layer contradicts

questions.explanation: A cross-section is a sequence, and a sequence is dated by what each layer could have been. A ground bound with a synthetic resin is a twentieth century campaign, or a modern intervention that treated the surface, and either way the object as it now stands is not an untouched sixteenth century surface. That is a statement about layers, and the two ways of resolving it are straightforward: the picture may be later than the catalogue says, or an older picture may have been stripped and reground, in which case the history of the object is longer than the catalogue assumed. What the finding does not do is reach downwards. A modern ground is exactly what you find on a genuine old panel that has been relined and reprepared, and nothing in the analysis says the paint beneath is a modern invention. Nor is a modern layer an accusation: conservators use these materials on a daily basis.
questions.hint: Ask which layer the binder belongs to, and what the layers underneath it can still be.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A copy standing in for a lost original
questions.learningObjective: state what a copy transmits and what it substitutes for
questions.stem: The original of a celebrated composition is lost, and a large painted copy in another collection is the only surviving witness to it. What does the copy carry?

options.text: The appearance of a design, and with it the authority to shape later opinion, while the material is its own
Nothing of the original, since a copy is a new object with no claim on the work it reproduces
options.misconception: denies a copy any evidentiary standing at all

options.text: The date and the hand of the original, since a faithful copy inherits the identity of what it copies
options.misconception: transfers authorship and date to the copy

options.text: The prices of both works, since a lost original and its copy are one object for any market
options.misconception: collapses two objects into one commercial object

questions.explanation: A copy is evidence about an appearance and nothing else, and that is a serious kind of evidence when nothing else survives. It fixes a composition that would otherwise be known only from descriptions, and because it is the object people actually look at, it accumulates authority its own date does not justify: the copy's condition and its restorations get described as if they were the original's, and its cropped or altered states get reconstructed. What the copy cannot carry is the material argument, since its pigments, its panel and its age are its own, and it cannot carry the working, since every decision in its surface belongs to the copyist's moment. A student reading a copy is therefore reading two things at once, the design that came down and the object that transmits it, and those need to be kept apart.
questions.hint: Ask what a copyist reproduces, and which of the original's facts belong to the original's material.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reversibility question about a restored area
questions.learningObjective: state what is asked when a restorer asks whether a fill is reversible
questions.stem: A restorer fills a loss in a painted panel and states that the fill is reversible because it can be removed with a solvent. What does the claim commit her to?

options.text: To the fill being findable, identifiable and removable without taking original material with it, and to that being documented
To the fill being invisible, since a reversible fill is one that a viewer cannot see at all
options.misconception: conflates reversibility with invisibility

options.text: To the original colour being restorable, since reversibility means the lost paint can be put back
options.misconception: reads reversibility as a promise of reinstating lost original material

options.text: To the panel returning to its untreated state, since a reversible treatment leaves no change at all
options.misconception: assumes a reversible treatment is a null intervention

questions.explanation: Reversibility is a claim about the future, and it has three parts. The fill must be findable, which means distinguishable from the original in normal examination and in raking light, since a fill a later conservator cannot see is a permanent loss in disguise. It must be identifiable, so that the material can be named and its solubility understood before anything is attempted. And it must be removable without carrying original material out with it, which is the hard part, because a solvent strong enough to lift a modern fill will also lift whatever it dissolves in an old ground, and that is a real risk rather than a theoretical one. The commitment also includes documentation, because reversibility nobody wrote down is not available to anybody. None of this requires the fill to be invisible, and a treatment can be honestly documented and honestly limited without pretending to be wholly reversible.
questions.hint: Ask what a later conservator has to be able to do, and what a solvent takes with it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Access restricted by a private collection
questions.learningObjective: state what a private holding does to scholarly access
questions.stem: A major private collection is open to visitors a few weeks in the year and to scholars by appointment, and publishes no catalogue. What does that arrangement do to the study of it?

options.text: It sets the pace and the subjects of research, since work proceeds only at the owner's convenience and on what can be seen
It protects the collection, since restricted access prevents damage that a busy public would soon cause
options.misconception: gives conservation as the whole of the effect and ignores the research cost

options.text: It improves the study, since a quiet room lets scholars examine the works more carefully than a crowd would allow
options.misconception: assumes quiet access is the same as working access

options.text: It has no effect, since a determined scholar can eventually see anything by travelling there repeatedly
options.misconception: denies the effect of a rule on the practical cost of research

questions.explanation: Access is a research resource, so a rule about it is a rule about what can be known. A few days a year, an appointment system and no catalogue mean that a study must be planned months ahead, that a researcher cannot revisit a work to check a question that arose later, and that the objects most likely to be examined are those the owner finds interesting, which is not the set most likely to be informative. The effect on scholarship is a distortion, and it is not a malicious one: a private owner has legitimate reasons of care, privacy and insurance. The useful response is not an accusation but an attempt to work within the arrangement, through published catalogues, through loans, and through the study of related works where the originals cannot be reached. What restricted access removes is the ability to check, and checking is most of what attribution research is.
questions.hint: Ask what a researcher loses that an ordinary visitor never needed in the first place.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Shared custody of a contested work
questions.learningObjective: state what shared custody settles and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Two institutions agree to hold a contested work jointly, each holding a share, and the work is displayed in turn at each. What has been settled and what has not?

options.text: The terms of present custody and display, while the claim of ownership and any claim for return stay open
Everything, since a joint holding settles the claim and the work is now owned equally by the two
options.misconception: reads an arrangement of custody as a settlement of title

options.text: Nothing, since a disputed work cannot lawfully be held until the claim is decided in court
options.misconception: supposes a judgment is a precondition of any arrangement

options.text: Only the insurance position, since shared custody is financial and the claims are unaffected
options.misconception: reduces the arrangement to insurance and leaves display untouched

questions.explanation: A shared-custody arrangement is an agreement about handling, and handling is exactly what it settles. The work is looked after, insured, conserved and shown, and the practical questions of who is responsible and where it hangs now have a written answer that keeps it accessible to the public. What it does not do is settle title, because the parties to such an agreement are usually in explicit disagreement about it, and agreeing to look after something jointly is not agreeing that it is yours. Nor does it settle a restitution claim, which is usually about a return to a country or a community rather than about who holds a share. The arrangement is best read as an honest way of keeping a contested object in public view while the dispute is argued, and its weakness is equally plain: it can defer a decision indefinitely, and the object remains a diplomatic question rather than a resolved one.
questions.hint: Ask what the two parties agreed to do, and whether that is the same as agreeing who owns the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The terms of a loan agreement
questions.learningObjective: interpret loan terms as conditions attached to an object
questions.stem: A loan agreement requires the gallery to hold the work at a stated temperature and humidity range, to give it its own case, to insure it for the full value, and to return it in the condition recorded, the lender keeping the right to withdraw it. What is that document doing?

options.text: Fixing the conditions the object will live under for the loan, so the lender's control is environmental, financial and temporal
Transferring ownership for the duration, since a loan of this length is in effect a gift with conditions attached
options.misconception: treats a loan as a transfer of title

options.text: Setting the admission price, since the return condition in the last clause is a term about how the work may be charged for
options.misconception: reads a condition of return as a condition of admission

options.text: Naming the artist, since a lender who specifies the case and the humidity has a particular maker in mind
options.misconception: infers an attribution from the lender's environmental conditions

questions.explanation: Every clause is a control exercised by somebody who is not going to be present, and together they describe the terms on which the object exists for the length of the loan. Temperature, humidity and a case are conservation requirements, set by the lender because the lender carries the risk of damage and cannot supervise the gallery's own practice. Insurance converts that risk into money and fixes the value that is protected, which is also why the valuation is a matter between the two institutions. The return condition closes the loop: the state recorded at the start is the state the work must be in at the end, and a difference is a claim rather than an accident. The right of withdrawal is a temporal control, and it matters most in practice when political circumstances change. None of this has anything to do with title or with the price of admission.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the risk of damage and who is not in the room to supervise.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A display curated by the community represented
questions.learningObjective: analyse what community curation redistributes
questions.stem: A display in a national museum is selected by a group drawn from the community the objects came from, and the labels give names and explanations the museum's own curators had not used, including one account the museum's research had rejected. What has been redistributed?

options.text: Authority over selection and wording, so the museum's account and another account of the same objects stand together in public
Ownership of the objects, since deciding how they are shown transfers title to the community that made them
options.misconception: turns a curatorial role into a transfer of ownership

options.text: The quality of the scholarship, since a community's account must be better researched than the museum's own
options.misconception: assumes community knowledge is automatically better evidenced

options.text: Nothing that matters, since the museum still controls the building, the security and the catalogue entry
options.misconception: dismisses a change in interpretation as irrelevant because the institution keeps the keys

questions.explanation: What has moved is authority over two specific things: which objects are shown, and what is said about them. That is a real redistribution of curatorial power, and it is why these displays matter: a museum's selection and wording are the result of professional training, funding and archival access, and a community may hold knowledge of use, of naming and of significance that the archive does not contain. The arrangement is therefore not a demotion of the museum but a widening of the evidence base, and it is compatible with a museum that still sets the conservation standards, holds the title and publishes the catalogue. Two cautions keep the reading honest. A community account is not automatically better researched, and the rejected explanation in this case may be wrong, which is why it is displayed alongside rather than instead. And the museum retaining the building is not a reason to call the change meaningless, since what a label says is the part the public reads.
questions.hint: Ask which two decisions a curator normally makes, and who has taken them here.

questions.topic: The objection and the answer on a blockbuster
questions.learningObjective: state the strongest objection to a large exhibition and its answer
questions.stem: A museum plans a large loan exhibition expected to draw crowds and to cost more than its education budget. First say the strongest objection, and then say the strongest answer to it.

options.text: That it removes the objects from study and decontextualises them, and that access for the many is itself a public good the museum exists to provide
That crowds damage the works, and that any exhibition drawing visitors is a conservation risk worth refusing
options.misconception: reduces the objection to damage, which is a solvable display problem

options.text: That it will make the museum rich, and that a profit makes the exhibition legitimate however it is arranged
options.misconception: makes money the measure of legitimacy

options.text: That it is unfair to the works left behind, and that the argument from access settles the case because access outranks every other consideration
options.misconception: grants access as an absolute that settles every objection

questions.explanation: The strongest objection is not about crowds or money. A loan exhibition takes objects out of their own buildings for months, so the scholars and the local audiences who use them cannot see them, and it hangs them in a thematic sequence that answers a question at the cost of the contexts the objects were made for. The strongest answer accepts that cost and argues that a collection which cannot be seen by the public that funds it has failed at one of its two jobs, and that a once-in-a-generation chance to reach people who will never visit the home galleries is worth a temporary gap in research access. The answer is weaker than it looks if it is treated as decisive, which is why the honest version of the argument is distributive: decide which loss matters more, for whom, and say so in public. Damage is a technical problem, profit is not a justification, and an appeal to access does not automatically outweigh the studies it postpones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Acquiring a contested work
questions.learningObjective: sequence due diligence and disclosure in an acquisition
questions.stem: A museum is offered a painting whose ownership between 1938 and 1945 cannot be traced. First say what has to be established before the offer is accepted, and then say what the museum owes the public if it goes ahead.

options.text: As much as can be established about the gap, and then a public statement of what is known, what is not, and what the museum has done about it
Nothing, since a work offered for sale in good faith cannot carry a claim, and the museum's only duty is to pay the seller
options.misconception: believes good faith by the seller ends the enquiry

options.text: That the work is by the artist, since a clear title and a secure attribution are the same question about a painting
options.misconception: conflates title with attribution as if one answer covered both

options.text: A refusal, since any gap in a provenance makes acquisition improper however well documented it is
options.misconception: makes a gap automatically disqualifying rather than a matter of judgement

questions.explanation: The first stage is enquiry, and the standard is not certainty, which is rarely available, but a serious attempt and an accurate account of the result. A gap in ownership during a period when works were removed by force or under duress is a fact about risk: somebody may have a claim, and the museum needs to know whether it would be acquiring an object that could be returned. A seller acting in good faith is not a shield, since a good-faith purchase can still be defeated, and title is a different question from authorship, which is why offering evidence of the artist does not answer it. The second stage is disclosure, and this is where museums have most often failed. A purchase made in silence transfers a contested object into a public collection and lets the public find out later, which damages the holding's legitimacy on a scale that outlives any single case. Publishing the gap, the searches made and the reasons for proceeding is what makes an imperfect decision defensible.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A restitution claim and the provenance it needs
questions.learningObjective: state what a restitution claim must establish from a provenance
questions.stem: A claim is made for the return of a painting said to have left a country under duress in the 1940s. First say what the provenance has to establish, and then say what follows if it cannot.

options.text: A documented chain of ownership through that period, and if it cannot be produced the museum must say so and weigh the other evidence on both sides
Only the date the painting was made, and if that is known the claim is settled by the date of the removal
options.misconception: reduces provenance to a date of making

options.text: Nothing at all, since a provenance can never be proved and every claim is settled by general practice rather than by evidence
options.misconception: denies that provenance is evidence at all

options.text: The buyer's good faith, and if that cannot be shown the claim fails, since only a dishonest purchaser owes anything
options.misconception: makes the claimant's case turn on the purchaser's state of mind

questions.explanation: A provenance is a chain, and the strength of the chain is what the claim rests on: who held the work, when, and on what record. For a claim about a removal under duress, the part that matters is the years in question, and a chain with a gap there is weaker than a chain without, so a missing link shifts the burden of explanation onto the holder rather than deciding the matter. Documents, and the absence of documents, both have to be weighed, and the legal frameworks written for this treat the relevant period as a defined one precisely so that the question has an end. If a complete chain cannot be produced, nothing follows automatically. The museum states what it knows and what it does not, and the other evidence, including the circumstances of the sale, the work's movement since and the position of the claimant, is weighed as well. A museum that treats an unprovable chain as a reason for silence has converted a hard question into an unanswerable one.
questions.hint: Ask what a chain of custody is made of, and where the claim's weight actually rests.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A condition report taken before a loan
questions.learningObjective: interpret a loan condition report as a baseline
questions.stem: A report made before a painting leaves on loan records two old fills, a small flaking area at the lower edge, a varnish that has yellowed unevenly, and photographs under raking light of every surface. What does it establish?

options.text: The state the work departs in, so that any change during the loan is attributable and any claim can be tested
That the painting is too fragile to travel, since two old fills and a flaking edge are disqualifying for any loan
options.misconception: treats recorded condition as a verdict on travelling

options.text: The value at which the work should be insured, since the extent of the fills and the varnish sets the sum
options.misconception: reads a condition record as a valuation

options.text: That the yellowed varnish is original, since an even change in varnish colour proves the original layer survives
options.misconception: reads an uneven varnish as proof of original surface

questions.explanation: The value of this report is entirely in its timing. Once the work is on the road, nothing that happens to it can be interpreted without a starting point, and a report written at the departure end gives the only starting point there is. That is why it is so detailed: two old fills are recorded so that a new loss near one is not blamed on the journey, a flaking edge is recorded because flaking moves with vibration and temperature, and raking-light photographs make the surface relief comparable rather than remembered. An even yellowing would be evidence about the original varnish, but an uneven one usually means a varnish applied or renewed unevenly, which is a treatment question rather than an authenticity one. None of this decides whether the work may travel; that is a professional judgement made on the report, and the insurance value comes from a valuation exercise of quite a different kind.
questions.hint: Ask what a later report would be compared against, and why the photographs are taken in raking light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A display case environment log
questions.learningObjective: interpret an environmental log as a conservation requirement
questions.stem: A gallery log for a case containing a wooden panel records a steady temperature with relative humidity moving between 40 and 65 per cent over three months, and daylight excluded except for a low-output lamp at 40 lux. What do the figures indicate?

options.text: That the case is buffering the room against a wider swing, since a narrow range matters more to wood than a perfect constant
That the case is failing, since a humidity range of twenty-five points is far outside the acceptable band for any object
options.misconception: treats variation as failure rather than as a range the case controls

options.text: That the light level is too low for visitors, since forty units of light is below what a painting requires to be seen
options.misconception: treats a conservation limit as a display failure

options.text: That the panel is being displayed in a temporary show, since permanent cases are never logged at this detail
options.misconception: infers a show's status from the existence of a log

questions.explanation: Read the log as a statement of two controls and their tolerances. The temperature is steady, which is the easy half, since a case in a conditioned gallery sits inside the building's own comfort. The humidity figure is the interesting one, and a range of 40 to 65 is a swing that a case exists to absorb: a wooden panel responds to the moisture it takes from the air, and it responds by swelling, shrinking, and opening and closing the joins, so what matters is not a single number but that the variation is bounded and slow. That is what a buffer of sealed material and a stable microclimate buys. The light figure is a conservation limit and a display decision at once, since light damage to colour is cumulative and irreversible, so a low-output lamp is a deliberate trade. A range is not a failure, and a quiet case is not thereby a temporary one.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a wooden panel as the moisture in the air around it changes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of acquiring a contested work
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a contested acquisition
questions.stem: A museum is considering a painting with a gap in its ownership history. Put these five steps into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Publish what was found, what was not, and the reasons for proceeding, so the decision is on the public record
Take the decision in the museum's own governing body, which carries the responsibility for a contested acquisition
Trace the ownership through the period in question, using the sale records, the published literature and the archives
Have the file reviewed by specialists in the field and by whoever advises the museum on legal questions
Examine the object itself, establishing its condition, its materials and its date before the money is discussed

questions.explanation: The order is set by what each step depends on. Tracing the ownership comes first because everything else, including whether an offer is worth considering at all, turns on what the chain shows, and a search begun after the money is agreed has already lost its freedom. Review follows, since specialists and legal advisers need the file rather than the object, and their task is to say what the gap does and does not permit. Then the examination, because a decision to acquire is a decision about a particular object, and a work whose materials or condition undermine the identification changes what is being bought. The governing body decides, and it decides on the assembled file rather than on the deal. Disclosure is last and is not optional: a contested object entering a public collection silently, and being discovered later, does more damage to the museum's standing than the original claim would have.
questions.hint: Ask what each step needs in hand before it can be done, and which step is not a step in the transaction at all.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of preparing an exhibition
questions.learningObjective: sequence the work of preparing a loan exhibition
questions.stem: A loan exhibition is being prepared. Put these five steps into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Write the labels and the catalogue, once the objects, the loans and the arguments are settled
Design the sequence and the cases, since the display conditions follow from what each object needs
Agree the loans in writing, with the conditions, the insurance and the transport settled before anything moves
Settle the argument the exhibition will make and identify the objects it needs, before anything is promised to a lender
Install and check the environment, since the conditions have to be right before the objects are brought in

questions.explanation: The work runs outward from the argument to the building. The exhibition begins with a claim about a body of material, and everything after that is a consequence: which objects are needed, which lenders must be approached, and what the loans will cost in conditions and in time. So loans are negotiated and agreed in writing, because a loan is a legal arrangement with a lender's terms attached and an oral agreement binds nobody. The sequence and the cases follow, and they are a conservation document as much as a design, since a fragile work on open display for four months dictates its own case, its light level and its neighbours. The labels and the catalogue come after the objects and the argument are fixed, since text written earlier has to be rewritten. Installation is last, with the environment checked and held steady before the works are brought in, because a room that is still adjusting is a room that will damage what is put into it.
questions.hint: Ask what the display cannot be decided until is settled, and what must be right before the objects arrive.

questions.topic: The life of a loan from report to return
questions.learningObjective: sequence a loan from condition report to return report
questions.stem: A panel is on loan to another institution for six months. Put these five steps into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Examine the object at the end of the loan, write the return report, and hand the work back
Write the condition report and photograph the work before it is packed, so the state at departure is on record
Check and hold the gallery's environment before the crate is opened and the work is installed
Sign the agreement, with the value, the conditions, the transport and the return date written into it
Pack and transport under agreed conditions, with the crate built and the route chosen for its handling

questions.explanation: The order runs from paper to object and back to paper, and the logic is that each step is the evidence for the next. The agreement first, because the value, the conditions, the transport and the return date are what the rest of the process is conducted under, and a loan begins when it is signed rather than when the van arrives. Then the condition report, taken and photographed while the work is in the building and before it is packed, since once it is in a crate the surfaces that matter cannot be examined. Transport follows, packed and routed to the agreed specification. At the other end the environment is checked and left holding before the crate is opened, because a work acclimatised in a cold van must not meet a warm room and a room still settling is worse than either. The closing report mirrors the opening one, and the two together are what makes a claim about damage discussable at all.
questions.hint: Ask which step is the evidence for the next, and what cannot be examined once a work is in a crate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wall text is an argument
questions.learningObjective: explain a wall text as an interpretive decision rather than a caption
questions.stem: Explain why a wall text is a piece of interpretation rather than a label, and work through the decisions it makes that no object can make for itself.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what distinguishes a wall text from a caption. A caption names an object: maker, title, date, medium, credit line. Those are fields in a record, and where they are known they can be printed without anyone forming an opinion. A wall text does something a caption cannot, because it has to be read by somebody standing in front of an object in a room with other objects in it, and it has to make that room say something. That means it selects, and every selection is an argument. The text for a portrait of an unknown sitter in an anonymous dress will decide whether to call the sitter a woman, a member of a family, a servant or a person whose identity the museum is still researching, and each word makes a claim about status and about what the museum knows. The title is the sharpest case. A modern descriptive title is a decision, and if it differs from the historical one, the difference is a claim that the historical one obscured something. Then there is the date. Museum practice of leaving a century off a work is a substantive statement that the evidence will not carry a decade, and the text has to say so rather than print a false precision. Selection extends to context as well: a work is described in relation to the period, the patron, the workshop or the street, and each of those relations is chosen among several that could be asserted. Now say what makes the text an interpretation rather than a description. It is because every one of those decisions could have gone another way, and a reader who disagrees has to be able to see what the alternative would have been. The counter-examples show the principle from the other side. A text that simply repeats the catalogue entry has made no interpretive decision at all, and has also forfeited the only thing a text in a gallery can do that a printed catalogue cannot, which is meet the visitor where they are standing. And a text that hides a known and serious problem with a work, an unresolved attribution, a disputed ownership, or damage that has been heavily restored, is not neutral for being short: silence is a decision that the visitor did not need to know, and it is the decision with the most authority, because nothing on the wall contradicts it. The practical test is simple and worth stating as the conclusion. Ask what the text asserts that the object does not, and ask what a different curator would have written. If nothing could have been written differently, there was no interpretation in the room, only a list.

questions.explanation: A full answer distinguishes caption from interpretation, works through at least two concrete decisions the text makes, and closes on the test of whether a different curator would have written it differently. A weak response treats a wall text as neutral information.
questions.hint: Ask what the text asserts that the object itself does not, and what a different curator would have written.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a digital surrogate is an interpretation
questions.learningObjective: explain the losses a surrogate carries as choices
questions.stem: Explain why a digital image of a painting is an interpretation of that painting, and list the decisions a viewer should distrust it for.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the surrogate is. It is a set of numbers produced by a camera, a lens, a light source, a colour profile and a choice of file, and the numbers then arrive on a screen that has its own characteristics. Nothing in that chain is neutral and each link can change what the viewer believes they are seeing. Colour is the most obvious and the most important. A camera without a calibration target records the light as its own sensor interprets it, a monitor is set by whoever installed it, and the difference between a warm-tinted screen and a cool one is larger than many of the colour decisions the painter made. So a reproduction of a painting whose reputation depends on a shift from a thin warm glaze to an opaque cool lead white can misrepresent the work's central effect, and the error is not always in the painter's favour. Take scale next, because it is the loss that viewers are least able to detect. A photograph of a large panel printed at a convenient size produces a picture of a picture, and a visitor who has only ever seen it will form a false sense of the object as something to be taken in at arm's length rather than something standing in a room. Surface is the third. Relief, impasto, craquelure, the grain of a wooden support and the bloom of an old varnish are all lost or flattened, and each of them is evidence: relief shows how a passage was worked, cracks record how the panel moved, and a varnish records a history of treatment. What a surrogate cannot do is substitute for looking, which is why it is indispensable to scholarship and inadequate to judgement. Now say how it should be used, and this is where the argument earns its conclusion. A surrogate is a legitimate research tool, because comparison of many images at a consistent scale and colour is something no gallery visit can do: it is how a student checks whether a hand recurs, how a curator tests a chronology, how a forger's copy differs from its prototype. It is a legitimate access tool, and for a damaged or inaccessible object it may be the only image anyone sees, which carries an obligation to say so on the page. What it is not is a record of fact. Its distortions are consistent enough to be repeated, so an error can acquire the authority of a citation, which is why a published surrogate should carry its capture conditions: the scale, the colour treatment, whether the light was raking or frontal, and what was not photographed. The test to end with is blunt. If two surrogates of the same painting disagree about a colour, the disagreement is information about the surrogates, not about the painter, and a reader who treats the image as the object will have learned something false with great confidence.

questions.explanation: A full answer identifies the capture-to-screen chain as the source of the distortions, names colour, scale and surface as the principal losses, and ends with the legitimate uses of a surrogate. A weak response says only that images are less accurate than the object.
questions.hint: Ask what stands between the object and the pixels, and which of the painter's decisions that chain can change.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Four kinds of interpretive text and their audiences
questions.learningObjective: compare a wall text, a curator's statement, a catalogue essay and a didactic panel
questions.stem: Compare a wall text, a curator's statement, a catalogue essay and a didactic panel: what audience does each assume, and what authority does each claim?

answer.exemplar: Take them in order of how far the reader is assumed to be from the museum, because that distance is what sets the register. A didactic panel is written for somebody who has not yet decided that art is interesting. It assumes no prior knowledge, a short attention span and a good reason to be looking, so it uses a question, an object that can be handled or a picture that can be examined, and it arrives at one idea. Its authority is practical: it claims that this is a good way to begin. A wall text assumes a visitor who has come to look and can read a paragraph, and it is written beside the object, so it must be true of the object in front of the reader and it must not be contradicted by anything else in the room. Its authority is the museum's, and it is the authority that a curious visitor is most likely to accept. A curator's statement is written before the exhibition exists, and it is addressed to a reader who will not see the rooms: it defends the choice, sets out the argument, and it is where the institution says what it thinks the material means. Its authority is institutional and its purpose is persuasion, which is why it is often more confident and more sweeping than the labels it produces. A catalogue essay is written for a reader who may never visit and who has paid, and it is a scholarly document: it argues from evidence, it cites, and it takes a position that other scholars are expected to contest. Its authority is the argument, and it is the only one of the four that a reader is positioned to answer. Then set out what follows, because the differences are practical rather than stylistic. The panel is written last and for the least expert reader, and it is often the only text that reaches anyone who has not been to the museum before. The wall text must agree with the catalogue, since a visitor with both in hand who finds them contradicting each other learns to distrust the museum. The statement and the essay will not always agree, and when they do not the disagreement is usually about how far the argument should be pushed, which is a legitimate thing to publish. And the shared rule is that all four are interpretations: each one selects, and a reader who wants to know what was left out should read them against each other rather than accept any of them as the neutral voice of the institution.

questions.explanation: A full answer distinguishes the four by assumed knowledge, position in the exhibition's life, and claimed authority, then draws a practical consequence. A weak response treats them as the same text at four lengths.
questions.hint: Ask who each text assumes is reading it, and at what point in the exhibition's life it is written.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photograph does to a work
questions.learningObjective: explain how reproduction reframes the object it depicts
questions.stem: Explain how a photograph of a work can change what the work is taken to be, and why this matters for an object whose public image is now mostly photographic.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the fact that a photograph is a picture of a picture, and that it enters the world without the original. A painting is an object standing in a room, at a size, in a light, with a frame and a history, and a photograph is a rectangle of tone on paper that can be moved anywhere, printed at any size and reproduced in millions. That transfer does not preserve the work, it re-describes it, and the re-description has effects. Take framing first. A photograph crops, and a crop is an editorial act: the whole point of a portrait's setting may be the doorway and the wash hanging at the edge, and a plate made to fit a page can remove both. Lighting is the second. A painting made to be seen in a candlelit chapel and a painting made to be seen in a top-lit room are read differently, and a single photograph taken under electric light sets the terms for every reproduction that follows it. Third, colour, where a plate made from a fading dye or from a book illustration will carry a cast that a generation of students then learns as the painter's palette. Now consider the two structural effects this has. A photograph detaches the image from the object, so a public can hold a picture of a work in mind that differs from the work, and where the photograph has become the familiar version the object is now the copy. And a photograph fixes a moment, which makes a work look simultaneous when it is not, and makes its present state permanent in the past tense, since the panel is still being cleaned, relined and damaged while the image is a single afternoon's exposure. Neither effect is a scandal, and the photograph is indispensable: it is how a collection is taught, how an object is published, how a distance is crossed, and how a work whose condition is deteriorating remains legible. The conclusion is about proportion rather than preference. A reproduction should be described as a photograph of a work, with its conditions given, so that a reader knows what has been left out and what has been added. Where the photographic image and the object are in conflict, that conflict is itself evidence: of a changing varnish, a campaign of restoration, or a cropped original, and it is the sort of evidence that examination of the object exists to produce. The test to leave with is that the photograph is a witness, not the work, and a witness whose account has to be checked against the thing it describes.

questions.explanation: A full answer names cropping, lighting and colour as the editorial acts, then draws the two structural consequences of a detached and fixed image. A weak response says only that photographs are less accurate.
questions.hint: Ask what a photograph leaves out of frame, and what it fixes about a work that is still changing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Adding the lost rings to a tree-ring date
questions.learningObjective: compute a felling bound from a dated ring and the rings lost at the edge
questions.stem: The outermost preserved ring of a panel is dated to 1748, the bark edge is missing, and five further rings are estimated to have been removed when the plank was cut. What is the earliest year in which the tree can have been felled?
questions.explanation: A tree adds one ring a year, and the ring that was outermost before the plank was cut is the last one the tree grew before it was felled. The preserved ring is dated 1748, so the tree had already produced that ring when the plank was sawn, which means the plank was cut after 1748 and not in 1748 itself. Five further rings are missing at the edge, and each of those is a year the tree went on growing after the last preserved one, so the felling cannot be earlier than 1748 plus 5, which is 1753. The second route agrees: counting from the felling backwards, the five missing rings occupy 1749, 1750, 1751, 1752 and 1753, so 1753 is the first year in which all of them exist. This is why a careful report gives a bound rather than a date, and why the estimate of lost rings has to be stated: it is the difference between an earliest possible felling and the year the last visible ring happened to fall in.
questions.hint: Add one year for each missing ring to the year of the last preserved ring.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Scale of a reproduction against the original
questions.learningObjective: compute the scale of a reproduction from the original's height
questions.stem: A full-page reproduction shows a painting 2.4 metres high as an image 24 centimetres high. What is the scale of the reproduction?
questions.explanation: Scale is a ratio of like to like, so the units have to be brought together first. The painting is 2.4 metres high, which is 240 centimetres, and the image is 24 centimetres high, so the ratio is 24 divided by 240, which is one tenth. Stated the other way, as a scale, the reproduction is one to ten. The check is that multiplying 240 centimetres by 0.1 gives 24 centimetres, which is the printed image. The number matters because a reproduction's scale is a fact about the reproduction, not about the work, and it is routinely left off prints. A reader who sees only the reproduction forms a wrong sense of the object: a 2.4 metre painting is a body-sized presence, and a quarter-scale print makes it look like a picture for a wall. This is why a catalogue reproduction of a large work should state its scale, and why two reproductions of the same painting at different sizes may show the same crop with quite different effects.
questions.hint: Convert the painting's height to centimetres, then divide the printed height by it.
